ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
While exploring outer space, Darth Vader comes upon a purely reflective spherical planet with radius $R_{p}=$ $40,000 \mathrm{~m}$ and mass $M_{p}=8.128 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$. Around the planet is a strange moon of orbital radius $R_{s}=$ $6,400,000 \mathrm{~m}\left(R_{s} \gg R_{p}\right)$ and mass $M_{s}=9.346 \times 10^{19} \mathrm{~kg}\left(M_{s} \ll M_{p}\right)$. The moon can be modelled as a blackbody and absorbs light perfectly. Darth Vader is in the same plane that the planet orbits in. Startled, Darth Vader shoots a laser with constant intensity and power $P_{0}=2 \times 10^{32} \mathrm{~W}$ at the reflective planet and hits the planet a distance of $\frac{R_{p}}{2}$ away from the line from him to the center of the planet. Upon hitting the reflective planet, the light from the laser is plane polarized. The angle of the planet's polarizer is always the same as the angle of reflection. After reflectance, the laser lands a direct hit on the insulator planet. Darth Vader locks the laser in on the planet until it moves right in front of him, when he turns the laser off. Determine the energy absorbed by the satellite. Assume the reflective planet remains stationary and that the reflective planet is a perfect polarizer of light.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure there is a large gray circle representing the reflecting planet, and outside the circle there is a dashed circular orbit representing the satellite orbit; the black dot on the left represents Darth Vader, and a horizontal arrow shoots from left to right onto the left-side surface of the planet. The visible horizontal dashed line in the figure is at the height of the incident laser and the impact point, and is not the horizontal line where the planet's center is located; the nearby Rp/2 label indicates the vertical offset between this incident/impact height and the horizontal line where the planet's center is located. The reflected light shoots from the planet surface toward the small gray circular satellite on the orbit, and the satellite is located on the upper-left orbit. Reasoning: According to the problem statement and the image, set the center of the reflecting planet as the origin, and take the incident laser direction as horizontal. The laser hits a point on the spherical surface, and its impact parameter relative to the “straight line from Darth Vader to the planet center” is b = Rp/2. Let theta denote the angle corresponding to the geometric deflection of the spherical-surface normal at that point relative to the incident centerline, then the initial angle satisfies sin(theta0)=b/Rp=1/2, so theta0=pi/6. When the satellite moves from the position where it is initially hit by the reflected light to directly in front of Darth Vader, the reflected-light direction turns from the initial direction to the forward return direction, and the geometric reflection relation gives that the change in reflected-light direction is twice the change in mirror-surface normal angle, therefore dphi = -2 dtheta. The satellite approximately undergoes circular motion around the stationary large planet, with angular velocity omega = sqrt(G Mp/Rs^3), so dt = |dphi|/omega = 2 dtheta/omega. The planet is an ideal polarizer, and the polarizer angle is the same as the reflection angle, therefore the power reaching the satellite is, by Malus' law, P(theta)=P0 cos^2(theta). The satellite is a blackbody and absorbs all light reaching it, so the total absorbed energy is E = integral P(theta) dt = (2P0/omega) integral_0^(pi/6) cos^2(theta) dtheta. Integral: integral cos^2(theta)dtheta = theta/2 + sin(2theta)/4, therefore from 0 to pi/6 it gives pi/12 + sin(pi/3)/4 = pi/12 + sqrt(3)/8. Multiplying by the preceding 2P0/omega gives E = (P0/omega)(pi/6 + sqrt(3)/4). Substituting numerical values: omega = sqrt((6.674e-11)(8.128e24)/(6.4e6)^3) ≈ 1.44e-3 s^-1. Thus E ≈ (2.0e32 / 1.44e-3)(0.5236 + 0.4330) ≈ 1.33e35 J.
